summary: Records the process and findings of the AAA working group panel that evaluated proposed protocols against the AAA network access requirements in RFC 2989.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3127 is the record of an evaluation, not a protocol. A panel of the AAA working group checked four candidate protocols, SNMP, Radius++, Diameter and COPS, against the network access requirements in RFC 2989, and scored each requirement as met fully, partly or not at all. Two of the four passed, and the panel slightly preferred Diameter.

questions: which aaa protocol did the ietf panel prefer
subtitle: How a panel of the IETF working group scored four candidate protocols against the network access requirements

tldr.problem: The IETF needed a protocol for authentication, authorization and accounting, the service that decides who may connect to the network and bills for what they use, and four candidate protocols had been submitted.
tldr.mechanism: A panel of seven people re-checked every requirement in RFC 2989 against the documents it came from, then scored each of the four proposals requirement by requirement as total, partial or failed compliance, using a brief written from each side.
tldr.outcome: The panel found SNMP and Radius++ not acceptable, and Diameter and COPS acceptable with minor and minor-to-medium engineering. It expressed a slight preference for Diameter, but noted that Diameter's use of SCTP puts SCTP on the critical path.

facts.label: Scores used per requirement
facts.value: T for total, P for partial, F for failed compliance

facts.label: Final verdict scale
facts.value: 4: Not Acceptable, Acceptable Only For Accounting, Acceptable with Engineering, Fully Acceptable

today: RFC 3127 is an Informational memo from June 2001 that has not been obsoleted or updated. It records a panel evaluation rather than a protocol, and it is explicit that the findings were not revised after the June 2000 Pittsburgh meeting where they were presented. Its conclusion was a slight preference for Diameter over COPS, with the note that Diameter's use of SCTP puts SCTP on the critical path.

sections.title: What the Panel Was Asked to Do
sections.content:
This memo represents the process and findings of the Authentication, Authorization and Accounting working group panel that evaluated protocols proposed against the AAA Network Access Requirements, RFC 2989. The abstract adds a caveat: due to time constraints of the report, the document is not as fully polished as it might have been, but it remains mostly in this state to document the results as presented.

Section 1 explains why the document looks the way it does. The original draft was rushed to meet the publication deadline of the June 2000 Pittsburgh meeting, and because that meeting had passed by the time the document was revised, the authors did not wish to substantially revise the findings, so as not to give the appearance of changing information after the presentation. Only additional descriptions of the process, formatting, layout editing and errors of fact were corrected in later revisions.

The process began after the working group was rechartered and the requirements document passed Last Call, with a solicitation for protocol submissions issued on 13 April 2000 to the working group's mailing list and to other IETF lists related to AAA, including NASREQ, Mobile IP, RAP and SNMPv3. Candidate authors were asked to notify the chairs of their intent to submit by 1 May 2000. Submissions and compliance description documents were to be sent as Internet Drafts by 1 June 2000, and to be considered as a candidate a submission needed an unqualified statement that it was an Internet standard, as described in RFC 2026.

The chairs formed an evaluation team, announced on 20 May 2000, whose job was to put together an Internet Draft documenting their evaluation. The goal was to have a first draft available before the 14 July 2000 submission deadline for IETF 48. Mike St. Johns was asked to chair the team, the chairs of the related working groups joined it, and further members were chosen to represent network operators as well as developers of AAA client and server software. The IESG advised the team.
sections.plainLanguage: The working group asked for protocol submissions, got four, and then formed a panel to judge them. The report is deliberately unpolished, because the authors did not want the findings to look as though they had been changed after the meeting where the results were presented.

sections.title: How the Proposals Were Evaluated
sections.content:
The evaluation process had three distinct phases. First, validate the AAA requirements document against the base requirements documents for NASREQ, MOBILEIP and ROAMOPS. Second, evaluate each of the SNMP, Radius++, Diameter and COPS proposal claims against the validated requirements. Third, provide final recommendations based on a side by side comparison for each proposal on a requirement by requirement basis.

The requirement validation was fairly mechanical: the evaluator checked what was said in the requirements document and verified that the references and supporting text in the base document supported the requirement as stated. Where a reference was wrong, too general, missing or otherwise unsupported, the requirement was either deleted or downgraded. The group then used the requirements document as modified by those findings to evaluate the proposals.

For each of the four proposals, the chair assigned two panel members to write evaluation briefs. One wrote a PRO brief and could take the most generous interpretation of the proposal, granting benefit of doubt. The other wrote a CON brief and was required to use the strictest criteria. Each brief looked at each individual requirement and judged how close the proposal came to meeting it, scoring the item as an F for failing to meet the requirement, a P for partially meeting it, or a T for totally meeting it. The proposals were scored only on the information presented, so a protocol might actually meet a requirement in practice but score lower if the proposal did not state, describe or reference how it was met.

The panel met by teleconference to discuss each proposal and its two briefs, then went through each requirement line by line as a group before members gave their own line-by-line evaluations, which determined the consensus result. A final meeting compared the results for the four proposals and checked that the criteria had been consistent. Each member then gave a final summary for each protocol, scored as either Not Acceptable, Acceptable Only For Accounting, Acceptable with Engineering or Fully Acceptable, with the size of the engineering noted as small, medium or large. The scores indicated the opinion of the team member, who might have taken into account background knowledge or additional issues not captured in the minutes.

The panel was allowed to use only the source documents, the requirements document and the proposals, or documents referenced by them. If it was not written down, it generally did not exist, and the cutoff for accepting information was 1 June 2000.
sections.plainLanguage: Each proposal got one brief arguing for it and one arguing against it, then the whole panel argued through the requirements one by one and agreed a score for each. The rule was that only what the documents actually said counted.

sections.title: How the Four Protocols Scored
sections.content:
The evaluation is reported requirement by requirement. The sub-section numbers correspond to the requirements document's own section and item numbers. A T means total compliance, meeting all requirements fully, a P means partial compliance, meeting some requirements, and an F means failed compliance, not meeting the requirements acceptably. Where two scores are shown, such as P/T, the panel was split.

On the general requirements, all four protocols scored T for certificate transport and for carrying service specific attributes. They all scored T for running over IPv4, and T except for SNMP for running over IPv6. Diameter and COPS scored T for scalability, where SNMP was downgraded for a lack of detail on how the current agent model would be adapted to a client request based transaction, and where the Radius proposal did not address the problem adequately. All four were marked down for fail-over, the group noting it did not think any protocol did well in that requirement, with insufficient work done on link failure detection and primary server recovery. SNMP and Radius++ both failed auditability, and SNMP also failed data object integrity and support for proxy and routing brokers, where the panel noted that Diameter was the only protocol to attempt to address that area to any fair extent.

On authentication, all four scored T for NAI support, CHAP support, EAP support and PAP or clear-text passwords. On authorization, all four scored T for the reject capability and for precluding Layer 2 tunnelling, and all four scored T for real time accounting, accounting record extensibility, guaranteed delivery, accounting timestamps and dynamic accounting. The sharpest disagreements were in the Mobile IP group, where SNMP failed firewall friendliness, Radius++ scored T, and Diameter and COPS scored P. The panel's explanation was that not making the firewall look into packets much beyond the application port number counts as firewall friendly, which puts SNMP and COPS at a disadvantage because you must look far into the packet to understand the intended operation, while Diameter carries the disadvantage of SCTP, which was not well deployed or recognised at the moment. The group also did not look at NAT friendly issues.
sections.plainLanguage: Every requirement got a score for every protocol. The protocols were close on authentication and accounting, and far apart on the general requirements, where SNMP and Radius++ failed several and Diameter and COPS scored well.

sections.title: The Verdict on Each Protocol
sections.content:
SNMP is generally not acceptable as a general AAA protocol. There may be some utility in its use for accounting, but the amount of engineering needed to turn it into a viable authentication and authorization protocol argues against further consideration.

Radius++ is not considered acceptable as an AAA protocol. There is a fairly substantial amount of engineering required to make it meet all requirements, and that engineering would most likely result in something close to the functionality of Diameter.

Diameter is considered acceptable as an AAA protocol. There is some minor engineering required to bring it into complete compliance with the requirements, well within short term capabilities, and it might also benefit from the inclusion of a broader data model in the style of COPS.

COPS is considered acceptable as an AAA protocol, with some minor to medium engineering required to bring it into complete compliance with the requirements.

The panel expresses a slight preference for Diameter, based on the perception that the work for Diameter is further along than for COPS. However, using SCTP as the transport mechanism for Diameter places SCTP on the critical path for Diameter, which may ultimately result in COPS being a faster approach if SCTP is delayed in any way.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP and Radius++ did not pass. Diameter and COPS both passed, with a little work needed, and the panel leaned towards Diameter because more of it was already built.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo notes that AAA protocols enforce the security of access to the Internet. The design of these protocols, and this evaluation process, took many security requirements as critical issues for evaluation. A candidate protocol must meet the security requirements as documented, and must be engineered and reviewed properly as it is developed and deployed.
sections.plainLanguage: These protocols decide who gets on the network, so their security requirements were treated as pass or fail issues rather than extras.

sections.title: References and the Appendices
sections.content:
Section 6 lists the references the memo relies on: the AAA requirements document RFC 2989, and the work-in-progress comparison document submitted with each of the four proposals, alongside a wider comparison of RADIUS, Diameter and COPS.

Appendix A holds the summary evaluations, the consensus result for every requirement and every protocol in one table, using the requirement numbering of the requirements document. Appendix B is the panel's review of the requirements document itself, listing the entries that were deleted, downgraded or corrected because the base documents did not support them as written, for example the scalability clarification about tens of thousands of simultaneous requests, which the panel found unsupported, and the auditability requirement, which only the NASREQ document asked for. The panel also recommended relabelling the misleadingly titled shared secret not required requirement as something closer to dual application and transport security not required.

Appendix C holds the position briefs, a PRO evaluation and a CON evaluation for each of the four protocols. Appendix D holds the meeting notes, the minutes of five teleconferences held between 22 June and 11 July 2000.
sections.plainLanguage: The appendices hold the full working: the score table, the corrections the panel made to the requirements document itself, the arguments for and against each protocol, and the minutes of the five calls where the panel argued.
